kicker: UP FRONT · FIELD GUIDE · No. 1 IN A SERIES OF ONE
title: How to Lose Like a Victorian
dek: In the late nineteenth century, Britain decided that the finest man in the Empire was the gentleman amateur. He played for honor, not money. He never questioned the referee. He shook the winner’s hand as though he’d been looking forward to it all day. (He could afford to. The ideal was built partly to keep out working men who were paid to play, so take it with a grain of the salt Rome never used.) The Victorians, being Victorians, wrote all of this down. We have adapted their rules for your next trivia night, where you will lose.
summary: Ten Victorian rules for losing gracefully, drawn from Routledge’s etiquette manual, Cassell’s parlour games and the Corinthians, adapted for trivia night.

blocks.text: A manual of deportment for the defeated
Rule 1. Confess your weakness up front.

Routledge’s Manual of Etiquette instructs an indifferent card player to say so before he sits down. Every trivia team has this man. He announces, “Don’t look at me unless it’s sports or the nineties.” He then misses the sports question and the nineties question, with the serene conscience of someone who filed the proper paperwork.
Rule 2. Separate the married couples.

Routledge’s forbids married people from playing at the same table. It gives no reason, in the way that a sign reading DO NOT FEED THE BEARS gives no reason. The final question will be the capital of Portugal. One spouse will say Lisbon. The other will say, “Oh, now you know where Lisbon is,” and the answer sheet will be found the next morning, folded very small, in a coat pocket.
Rule 3. Forgive your teammate’s blunders, cheerfully.

Routledge’s again. If your teammate writes 1067 for the Battle of Hastings, let it stand. The Victorian scream was entirely internal; scholars believe this is what the muttonchops were for. A satirical manual on whist (bridge’s stuffier grandfather) from 1895 offers a loophole: once the hand is over, you may call your partner anything you like. The round ends at 8:15. Pace yourself.
Rule 4. The quizmaster’s word is final.

Victorian card players sent their disputes to a bystander with no stake in the game. Tonight that bystander is a 26-year-old named Tyler with a microphone, a laminated answer key and the moral authority of the Lord Chief Justice. If the key is wrong, the 1895 satire advises you to “revile the facts.” Revile them in the car.
Rule 5. Congratulate the winners in person.

Walk over. Shake hands. Say “well played” as though it costs you nothing, which, for a man with four thousand a year and a house in Shropshire, it didn’t. Expect the winners to ask if you’re doing a bit. You are. It’s called character.
Rule 6. Give back points you didn’t earn.

The Corinthians, England’s gentleman football club, reportedly refused to defend penalty kicks. The goalkeeper leaned against the post and let the ball in, because a gentleman never fouls on purpose and a penalty implied he had. C. B. Fry, their star, is credited with calling the penalty rule “a standing insult.” (Fry also claimed he was once offered the throne of Albania, so weigh his views accordingly.) If the host scores you a point by mistake, return it. Your teammates will look at you the way the Senate looked at Brutus. The Corinthians are not on your team.
Rule 7. Pay your forfeit.

Victorian parlour games ended in forfeits, and Cassell’s 1881 book of indoor amusements lists the going rates. Kiss your own shadow. Kiss the candlestick, a trick in which you ask a lady to hold the candle and then kiss her, which tells you all you need to know about who wrote the book. Cassell’s also insists that forfeits are greater fun than the games themselves, a sentence no loser has ever written. Buy the winners a round. Next to the candlestick, it’s a bargain.
Rule 8. Receive the consolation prize as you would a knighthood.

Cambridge’s math exams once closed with a ceremony for whoever came last: a wooden spoon, lowered on strings from the Senate House gallery until it dangled over his head as he took his degree. Over the decades the spoons grew, the way grudges do. The last one, in 1909, was an oar about a meter long, inscribed in Greek. Tonight’s consolation prize is half-price mozzarella sticks. Receive them as you would a knighthood. You got off easy.
Rule 9. Keep your mustache under control.

From 1860 to 1916 the British Army required soldiers to wear one. The general who finally scrapped the rule reportedly shaved his own off that same evening, which is the most Victorian possible way of saying “I’ve been waiting a long time to do that.” Keep a stiff upper lip. Note, however, that “stiff upper lip” is American, first printed in Philadelphia in 1811. So is the “booby prize,” from Michigan card parties of the 1880s, where one lucky loser took home a live mouse in a box. The Victorians borrowed both and never sent a thank-you note, which, per Routledge’s, is very bad form.
Rule 10. Do not post about it.
A gentleman amateur did not write a thread. He wrote a letter to The Times, which is a thread for people who own a hat.
